lead: Network topology studies only the shape of a circuit: which nodes each branch joins, not what the branch contains. Drawn this way a circuit is a graph. A spanning tree picked from the graph gives, in a fixed recipe, a complete set of independent KVL equations (one tie-set per chord) and of independent KCL equations (one cut-set per tree branch). The recipe always gives the right number of equations, which is why circuit simulators use it, and it covers circuits that cannot be drawn flat.
prereq: You need: node, branch, tree and chord from Network terminology.

blocks.text: Replace every element by a line (a branch or edge) between its two nodes (vertices). Some textbooks first replace ideal voltage sources by short circuits and ideal current sources by open circuits; here every element, source included, stays a branch. Give each branch an arrow for its positive current direction and the graph is oriented. A graph is connected if there is a path between every pair of nodes.

A tree is a connected set of branches that touches all n nodes and contains no closed path. Its branches are twigs; the remaining branches form the co-tree, and each of them is a link (chord). For a connected graph with n nodes and b branches:

blocks.where: These hold for a connected graph; a graph in k separate parts has n − k twigs. Many different trees exist, but every tree has the same counts.

blocks.text: The incidence matrix has one row per node and one column per branch, with +1 where the branch leaves the node, −1 where it enters, 0 elsewhere. Delete the reference node's row to get the reduced incidence matrix A; then A i = 0 is KCL at the other n − 1 nodes.

sections.h3: Tie-sets: one link, one loop, one KVL equation

blocks.text: Add one link to the tree and exactly one closed path appears: the link plus the unique tree path between its ends. This is a fundamental loop, and its set of branches is a fundamental tie-set. Orient the loop the same way as its link. There are b − n + 1 of them, and each contains a link that no other contains, so their KVL equations are independent.

Write them as a tie-set matrix B (rows: tie-sets; columns: branches; +1 if the branch arrow agrees with the loop direction, −1 if it opposes, 0 if absent). KVL is B v = 0. The link currents act as loop currents, and every branch current follows from them: i = Bᵀ IL. For the bridge in the figure (tree 4, 5, 6; links 1, 2, 3):

sections.h3: Cut-sets: one twig, one split, one KCL equation

blocks.text: A cut-set is a minimal set of branches whose removal splits a connected graph into exactly two parts; minimal means that putting back any one of them reconnects the graph. Remove one twig from the tree and the tree falls into two parts; the twig together with every link that joins the two parts is a fundamental cut-set. Orient it like its twig. There are n − 1 of them, one per twig.

Write them as a cut-set matrix Q (+1 if a branch crosses the cut in the twig's direction, −1 if against it). KCL is Q i = 0, and the twig voltages give every branch voltage: v = Qᵀ vt. For the same tree:

Each row of B and each row of Q share branches with signs that cancel (B Qᵀ = 0), so the b − n + 1 tie-set equations and n − 1 cut-set equations together are b independent equations. Tie-set analysis is the general form of mesh analysis, and cut-set analysis the general form of nodal analysis.

figure.caption: The oriented graph of the bridge circuit: four nodes, six branches. The chosen tree (solid) joins every node to D with no loop; each dashed chord closes one fundamental loop (tie-set), and cutting each tree branch isolates one node (cut-set).

examples.question: For the bridge circuit of the figure (branch 1: A to B, 20 Ω; 2: A to C, 20 Ω; 3: C to B, 10 Ω; 4: B to D, 2 Ω; 5: C to D, 8 Ω; 6: the 36 V source from D to A), use the tree {4, 5, 6} to write the tie-set equations, find all six branch currents and check them with the cut-set equations.
steps: Loop currents are the link currents I₁, I₂, I₃. From i = Bᵀ I<sub>L</sub>: i₁ = I₁, i₂ = I₂, i₃ = I₃, i₄ = I₁ + I₃, i₅ = I₂ − I₃, i₆ = I₁ + I₂.
Branch voltages (drop along the arrow): v<sub>k</sub> = R<sub>k</sub>i<sub>k</sub> for the resistors and v₆ = −36 V for the source, since its arrow runs from − to +.

Solve: I₁ = (36 − 2I₃)/22 and I₂ = (36 + 8I₃)/28. Substituting and multiplying by 308 gives 1008 − 56I₃ − 3168 − 704I₃ + 6160I₃ = 0, so 5400I₃ = 2160 and I₃ = 0.4 A. Then I₁ = 35.2/22 = 1.6 A and I₂ = 39.2/28 = 1.4 A.
Branch currents: i₁ = 1.6 A, i₂ = 1.4 A, i₃ = 0.4 A, i₄ = 2.0 A, i₅ = 1.0 A, i₆ = 3.0 A.
Cut-set check: twig 4: −1.6 − 0.4 + 2.0 = 0; twig 5: −1.4 + 0.4 + 1.0 = 0; twig 6: −1.6 − 1.4 + 3.0 = 0. The same numbers came out of the star-delta reduction of this bridge.
examples.answer: i₁ = 1.6 A, i₂ = 1.4 A, i₃ = 0.4 A, i₄ = 2 A, i₅ = 1 A and the source current i₆ = 3 A.

traps: Using n instead of n − 1 for the number of twigs, or b − n instead of b − n + 1 for the number of links.
Calling any loop a fundamental tie-set. A fundamental tie-set has exactly one link; the rest are twigs.
Calling any set of branches that separates the graph a cut-set. It must be minimal and leave exactly two parts.
Swapping the counts: tie-sets equal links (b − n + 1), cut-sets equal twigs (n − 1).
Ignoring orientation. In B and Q each entry is +1 or −1 by comparing the branch arrow with the loop or cut direction; a wrong sign corrupts the equation.

quiz.a: A tree is a connected set of branches touching every node with no closed path. Its branches are twigs; the branches not in the tree are links (chords).

quiz.q: Why does each link give exactly one fundamental loop?
quiz.a: A tree has exactly one path between any two nodes. The link plus that unique path closes one loop, and no other link is in it.

quiz.q: Why are there n − 1 fundamental cut-sets?
quiz.a: The tree has n − 1 twigs, and removing each twig splits the tree in two, defining one cut-set. So there is one fundamental cut-set per twig.

quiz.q: A connected graph has n = 6 and b = 10. Find twigs, links, fundamental tie-sets and fundamental cut-sets.
For the bridge graph with the tree {1, 4, 5}, list the links and the fundamental tie-set of link 6.
quiz.a: Links: 2, 3, 6. Link 6 runs from D to A; the tree path from A to D is A-B (1) then B-D (4). Tie-set of link 6: {6, 1, 4}, the loop D-A-B-D.

quiz.q: A student says a graph with n = 5 and b = 8 has 3 tie-sets and 5 cut-sets. Correct both.
quiz.a: Tie-sets = links = b − n + 1 = 4, not 3. Cut-sets = twigs = n − 1 = 4, not 5. The student used b − n and n.

beyond: Not for the exam. Circuit simulators store the incidence matrix and pick trees to build sparse equations; power-system programs use graph search to find islands, parts of a grid cut off from every generator. Kirchhoff's own 1847 paper used spanning trees to solve circuit equations, and the matrix-tree theorem that counts spanning trees carries his name. Search next for fundamental loop matrix, fundamental cut-set matrix and the matrix-tree theorem.
